title: The Manifest Split
protagonist: Marcus Feld, customs and logistics coordinator, container terminal night shift

options.A: The Combined Lane -- one generalist crew certified for both hazmat and reefer checks, no re-handling required
options.B: The Split Lanes -- two specialist crews, each faster at its own single check, but any dual-flagged container must be re-handled between lanes

not_found: A public, per-sailing hazmat/reefer flag-count breakdown for any specific real container terminal -- this is internal gate-scan/operational data no terminal publishes. Became MA1 (H=90, R=130, union=195), a disclosed scenario assumption.

A published per-container inspection-time figure specific to a terminal's own hazmat placard/documentation check or reefer plug/setpoint check, for either a generalist or specialist crew. Became MA2-MA5.
A published inter-lane container re-handle time (crane pull + yard move + re-queue) for any real terminal. Became MA6, informed by a real yard-crane-cycle floor (S3) but not equal to it.

A specific, dated real-world lithium-ion-battery-in-reefer hazmat reclassification bulletin naming an exact affected container count -- the FACILITATOR.md twist's +30-container reclassification is a disclosed scenario construction grounded in the real, ongoing regulatory reality that lithium-ion cells are IMDG Class 9 and increasingly shipped refrigerated, not a citation to one specific real bulletin.
scenario_constructions: Marcus Feld and the specific terminal in this case are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention (e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case, Priya Nakamura / FlowState).

Tonight's exact flagged-manifest counts (H=90, R=130, union=195) and the twist's +30-container reclassification are constructed to create a genuine, close decision within SPEC Section 2's ~20% balance margin; they are not derived from any single real terminal's actual sailing data.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific terminal's per-sailing hazmat/reefer flag breakdown -- this is internal gate-scan data. Set at a scale consistent with a mid-sized terminal processing a multi-thousand-TEU vessel call, where flagged cargo is a real but small fraction of the total manifest.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The whole comparison is sensitive to these counts -- a different union total or H/R split changes the intersection size Challenge D1 asks the student to find, which is the basis of the entire decision.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Combined Lane hazmat check time
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a generalist crew's per-container hazmat check time. Set higher than the specialist figure (MA4) to reflect that a crew certified for both hazmat and reefer procedures must stay ready to switch checklists container to container -- no terminal-specific figure exists to cite directly.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Combined Lane reefer check time
modeling_assumptions.basis: Same basis and sensitivity class as MA2, applied to the reefer half of the combined check.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Split Lanes hazmat check time
modeling_assumptions.basis: Set below MA2 to reflect a specialist crew running one procedure repeatedly rather than switching between two. No public source publishes a terminal-specific duration.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Split Lanes reefer check time
modeling_assumptions.basis: Same basis as MA4. A real, published pre-trip reefer inspection guide describes this class of check as short, on the order of a few minutes [S2], consistent with but not a direct source for this exact value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Re-handle time for a dual-flagged container
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a terminal's inter-lane transfer time. A real container-terminal productivity benchmark states top terminals reach >30 yard-crane moves/hour, a floor of ~2 minutes/move [S3]; a full re-handle (un-stack, yard-truck move, re-queue) is set above that floor as a disclosed assumption.

sensitivity_note: No SPEC Section 6 subject-matter sensitivity applies. This is an operations/compliance decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: The Combined Lane wins if the intersection of hazmat-and-reefer containers is large enough that The Split Lanes' re-handling cost outweighs its per-check speed advantage -- and a real, disclosed compliance-bulletin scenario (the twist) shows that threshold is not hypothetical: a modest reclassification of 30 containers pushes the intersection from 25 to 55, past the crossover point (x=40 at baseline H+R), and The Combined Lane's simplicity (no re-handling, ever) wins outright.
balance.argument_b: The Split Lanes wins on tonight's actual numbers (11.3% margin) because its specialist crews are faster at every single check, and tonight's intersection (25 containers, out of 195 total flagged) is not yet large enough for the re-handling cost to erase that per-check speed advantage.
balance.margin_basis: Compute total inspector-minutes for each configuration from Appendix C's per-container times applied to Appendix B's set sizes (via Appendix D's inclusion-exclusion intersection), convert to inspector-hours, then divide the union count (total distinct containers cleared, identical under either configuration) by each configuration's inspector-hours.
balance.twist_effect: A supplemental compliance bulletin reclassifies 30 previously reefer-only containers as also hazmat (refrigerated lithium-ion cell shipments). Those 30 are a subset of R, so the union (195) is unchanged but H rises to 120, which by inclusion-exclusion raises the intersection from 25 to 55 -- past the x=40 crossover point where the two configurations tie. Post-twist: A = 6.257, B = 5.924, a 5.61% margin, winner flips to The Combined Lane (A). Disclosed here and in sensitivity_model.py; never in case.md or FACILITATOR.md's student-facing sections.
balance.stability: Base margin (11.26%) is a direct, computable function of all five timing assumptions (MA2-MA6) via sensitivity_model.py. See sensitivity_disclosure[] -- every one of the five timing assumptions flips the winner or breaches the SPEC Section 2 20% cap at a +/-50% flex, which is a real, disclosed finding about how tightly this case's margin depends on undisclosed real-world per-container timing data, not a defect introduced by an unscoped sweep (H/R/union are deliberately excluded from FLEX -- see sensitivity_model.py's docstring).

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2 has no citable terminal-specific source; it is an irreducible scenario estimate for a generalist crew's per-container hazmat check time. Flexing +50% breaches the 20% cap (35.84%, B wins wider); flexing -50% flips the winner to A (15.35%, within cap). A facilitator should expect this to be one of the two most load-bearing assumptions.
MA3, same basis class as MA2. Flexing +50% breaches the cap (42.32%); flexing -50% flips the winner to A AND breaches the cap (24.68%). The single most load-bearing assumption in the model.
MA4, no citable terminal-specific source. Flexing +50% flips the winner to A without breaching the cap (6.44%); flexing -50% breaches the cap (36.40%, B wins wider).
MA5, informed only by a supplemental real source (S2) as a plausibility floor, not a direct citation. Flexing +50% flips the winner to A (9.82%, within cap); flexing -50% breaches the cap (42.98%).

MA6, informed only by a real crane-cycle floor (S3), not the full re-handle process. Flexing -50% breaches the cap (22.79%, B wins wider) but does not flip the winner; flexing +50% narrows the margin sharply (1.72%) without flipping it. This is the assumption the FACILITATOR.md twist deliberately does NOT flex directly -- the twist instead changes the intersection size (H), a structurally different and, per case.json.balance.twist_effect, actually more decisive lever.

deliverables.text: A labeled Venn diagram of tonight's flagged manifest: calculate the intersection from the given H, R, and union counts, and draw H, R, their overlap, and every region's correct count.
A total-inspection-time table for each lane configuration, using the per-container check times and the D1 intersection count, converted to inspector-hours.
A containers-cleared-per-inspector-hour comparison for each lane configuration and the percent margin between them.
A one-paragraph written recommendation naming the chosen configuration and addressing the empty-set edge case (no dual-flagged containers at all).

catalog.ask: Marcus has one night shift to clear a container ship's manifest: inspect every container on two separate hazmat and high-value lists twice, or once by combining them into a single set. Set theory says which containers actually need double-checking -- and which don't.
